result:
The repair shop at the end of the street fixed things that weren’t supposed to break.

Not clocks or kettles. There were other shops for those.

This one repaired the feeling of arriving home, the ability to enjoy a song after someone unkind had loved it, and the small but essential mechanism that lets a person say, “I don’t know,” without feeling diminished.

The proprietor was a woman named Ada. She wore a blue apron and kept a jar of mismatched buttons beside the till. These were not magical. She just liked buttons.

One wet Thursday, a man brought in his sense of wonder.

“It’s probably not worth fixing,” he said.

Ada laid it on a square of felt beneath the desk lamp. It looked like a little brass telescope, dented along one side.

“How long has it been like this?”

“Hard to say. I’ve been busy.”

She peered through it.

“Ah.”

“Bad?”

“Mostly clogged.”

“With what?”

Ada tipped the telescope over. A fine gray powder drifted onto the felt.

“Things you’ve already decided about.”

The man looked offended, then tired.

“Can you clean it?”

“Yes. But there’s a part you’ll need to replace yourself.”

She showed him a tiny empty slot near the eyepiece.

“What goes there?”

“A question you don’t already have an answer to.”

He considered this.

“Why is the world such a mess?”

Ada tried the question in the slot. It wouldn’t fit.

“That one appears to contain an answer.”

He stood by the window. Rain gathered on the awning and fell in irregular, heavy drops. Across the street, a pigeon was bathing in a puddle beside a perfectly adequate fountain.

“Why that puddle?” he asked.

There was a quiet click.

Ada looked through the telescope again, adjusted something with her thumbnail, and handed it back.

“What do I owe you?”

“Nothing today. The hinge is still loose. Bring it back next week.”

He put it carefully in his coat pocket.

Outside, he paused beside the fountain. The pigeon stopped bathing and watched him.

After a while, he crouched to look at the puddle.

From the shop, Ada saw him shift a few inches to the left, then to the right. She couldn’t tell what he’d found. She was tempted to go and see, but another customer had come in carrying a laugh that hadn’t sounded right for years.
